Disclaimer

HazardPulse forecasts are research estimates. They are not official forecasts, watches, warnings or advisories.

For warnings, use official sources

For warnings and every decision about your safety, follow the official agencies and your local emergency officials:

  • National Weather Service (weather.gov): tornado and severe weather warnings and all US weather.
  • Storm Prediction Center: severe weather outlooks and watches for the contiguous US.
  • National Hurricane Center: tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and East Pacific, and through its Central Pacific Hurricane Center, the Central Pacific.
  • Joint Typhoon Warning Center and your national meteorological service (for example the Japan Meteorological Agency or the India Meteorological Department) for storms elsewhere.
  • USGS Earthquake Hazards Program and your national geological survey for earthquakes.

What these numbers are

HazardPulse publishes probabilities produced by automated statistical and machine-learning models from public data. Where a model also produces an uncertainty range we show it; where it does not, we show the single number. No model predicts natural hazards perfectly, and HazardPulse does not guarantee the accuracy of any individual forecast.

HazardPulse does not issue official forecasts or warnings and does not replace the USGS, NOAA, the NWS or any government agency. Its forecasts must not be the sole basis for evacuation, sheltering or any emergency-management decision.

How to read a forecast

A 30% chance means the event is expected in about 3 of every 10 similar situations, and not in the other 7. A low chance is not a promise of safety, and a high one is not a certainty.

Compare a number with the usual rate for that place and window. A 20% chance of a magnitude 6+ earthquake within 30 days can be routine in one of the most active grid cells on Earth and exceptional in a quiet one.
